title: Keys, keyspace and expiry
summary: How keys are named and addressed, the generic keyspace commands, SCAN cursor semantics, TTL mechanics, and how active and lazy expiry actually delete keys.

blocks.body:
Everything in Redis lives under a key. Keys are binary-safe byte sequences — any
string up to 512 MB — but the exam cares less about that limit than about what a
good key name does for you: it makes the keyspace scannable, operations targetable,
and ownership obvious.

## Key naming conventions

The community-standard shape is `object-type:id:field`, with colons as namespace
separators:

```text
user:42                    a hash for user 42
session:a1b2c3             a session string
user:42:followers          the follower set of user 42
rate:api-key-9:2026-09-03  a daily counter
```

A consistent scheme pays off three ways:

- `SCAN` with `MATCH user:*` walks one logical family of keys.
- You can grant an ACL user access to `~user:*` and nothing else.
- Reading a key name tells you its role without a `TYPE` round trip.

Use dashes or dots inside segments, never a second separator style; a key scheme
you cannot pattern-match is a key scheme you cannot operate.

## Generic keyspace commands

These work regardless of value type:

| Command | Complexity | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EXISTS | O(1) | accepts multiple keys, returns how many exist |
| TYPE | O(1) | string, list, set, zset, hash, stream |
| DEL | O(N) | blocking — frees memory synchronously |
| UNLINK | O(1) | unlinks now, reclaims memory in a background thread |
| RENAME | O(1) | TTL travels with the key |
| PERSIST | O(1) | strips a key's TTL |
| RANDOMKEY, DBSIZE | O(1) | sampling and counts |

`DEL` versus `UNLINK` is a classic exam contrast. Both remove the key from the
keyspace in O(1) amortized time, but `DEL` also frees the value's memory right
there on the main thread — milliseconds of stall for a multi-gigabyte set — while
`UNLINK` detaches the key and lets the lazy-freeing background thread reclaim the
memory later. `UNLINK` is only an O(1) win when the value is actually large.

## KEYS and SCAN

`KEYS pattern` matches the whole keyspace in one O(N) sweep **on the main
thread**. On a production instance with millions of keys it blocks every other
command for the duration — a textbook production incident, and the exam knows it.

`SCAN` does the same job incrementally:

```redis
SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
1) "3412"                    the cursor to resume from
2) 1) "user:41"              a batch of candidate keys
   2) "user:42"
SCAN 3412 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
```

The cursor is an opaque position (an inverted bucket index, in the reverse-binary
scheme), and iteration ends when the server returns `0`. Points the exam tests:

- Per call, `SCAN` is bounded work — O(1)-ish for the returned batch, not O(N).
- A complete iteration is still O(N) over the whole keyspace, just spread across
  calls, so latency is amortized instead of concentrated.
- `COUNT` is a *hint* per round trip (default 10), not a hard batch size.
- `MATCH` filters after the scan, so it does not reduce how many keys are walked.
- `SCAN` also has per-structure variants — `SSCAN`, `HSCAN`, `ZSCAN` — for
  iterating a large collection incrementally.

**SCAN guarantees** (and their limits):

- A full iteration retrieves all keys that were present in the keyspace from
  start to end of the iteration — no key is missed if it existed the whole time.
- It may return the same key more than once: duplicate handling is the client's
  job.
- Keys added or removed *during* iteration may or may not be returned — the
  guarantee covers only keys present for the entire iteration.
- During a full rehash of the keyspace dict, `SCAN` walks both old and new tables,
  which is where the duplicate possibility comes from.

`SMEMBERS` on a large set blocks; `SSCAN` on the same set does not. Same rule
for every collection type.

## Expiry: the TTL command family

```redis
SET token:a1b2 "payload"
EXPIRE token:a1b2 3600        # seconds
PEXPIRE token:a1b2 1500       # milliseconds
EXPIREAT token:a1b2 1789000000  # absolute unix time (seconds)
TTL token:a1b2                # seconds left; PTTL for milliseconds
EXPIRETIME token:a1b2         # unix time when it dies (PEXPIRETIME in ms)
PERSIST token:a1b2            # remove the TTL, key becomes immortal
```

Return values worth memorizing:

- `TTL` returns `-1` when the key exists but has no TTL, and `-2` when the key
  does not exist at all.
- `EXPIRETIME` gives the absolute expiry as a unix timestamp.
- Redis 7 added `EXPIRE` options: `NX` (only if no TTL), `XX` (only if a TTL
  exists), `GT` (only if it extends), `LT` (only if it shortens).

## Active versus lazy expiry

Two cooperating mechanisms delete expired keys:

- **Lazy (passive) expiry**: when a client touches an expired key, Redis sees the
  expired timestamp, deletes it, and answers as if the key never existed. No cost
  unless the key is accessed — but an expired-forever unread key would linger.
- **Active expiry**: a background cycle runs roughly ten times per second,
  samples 20 keys from each keyspace's expires dict, deletes the expired ones,
  and if more than 25% of the sample was expired, immediately samples again. This
  bounds how long dead keys can accumulate unread.

So "expired" means "logically gone": reads never observe an expired key, but the
memory is reclaimed by whichever mechanism reaches it first. Expiry is stored as
absolute timestamps in a separate expires dict, which is why `TTL` survives a
restart that loads the key from a persistent snapshot.

## SET overwrites the TTL

The exam's favorite TTL trap: a plain `SET` on an existing key **clears its TTL**.

```redis
SET k "v1" EX 60
SET k "v2"            # TTL gone — k is now immortal
TTL k                 # -1
```

Any `SET` that does not carry `EX` / `PX` / `EXAT` / `PXAT` discards the old TTL.
To update a value and keep the countdown, either re-supply the expiry or use
`KEEPTTL`:

```redis
SET k "v2" KEEPTTL    # new value, old TTL preserved
```

Other writes behave differently: `HSET`, `LPUSH`, `SADD`, `APPEND`, `INCR` and
friends modify the value without touching the TTL. Only `SET` (and `GETSET`,
its ancestor) resets the clock by clearing it. `RENAME` moves the TTL with the
key; renaming A onto B replaces B, and B's old TTL dies with it.

## Big keys and O(N) hazards

A **big key** is any key whose value is huge — a string of tens of megabytes, a
hash or set with millions of fields. Big keys hurt three ways:

1. Any O(N) read (`HGETALL`, `SMEMBERS`, `LRANGE 0 -1`, `KEYS`) over them holds
   the event loop for the whole scan.
2. Deleting one on the main thread with `DEL` stalls everything; `UNLINK` (or
   `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`) moves the free off-thread.
3. They skew memory and shard balance: one giant key can dominate a node.

Find them before production does: `redis-cli --bigkeys` samples the keyspace per
type, and `MEMORY USAGE key` prices a single key. Mitigate by sharding the
concept across many small keys (`user:42:followers` rather than `followers`),
reading with cursor variants, and always deleting with `UNLINK` when size is
unknown.

## Exam takeaways

- Keys are binary-safe strings; a colon-namespaced, pattern-friendly scheme is
  what makes `SCAN MATCH` and ACL `~patterns` usable.
- `DEL` frees memory on the main thread; `UNLINK` hands it to a background
  thread — same result, different latency profile.
- `SCAN` guarantees completeness for keys present the whole iteration, permits
  duplicates, and says nothing about keys added mid-iteration; `KEYS` blocks.
- `TTL` returns -1 (no expiry) and -2 (missing key); `EXPIRETIME` returns the
  absolute expiry; `PERSIST` removes the countdown.
- Expired keys vanish from reads immediately (lazy) and from memory within
  bounded time (active sampling); a plain `SET` clears a key's TTL unless you
  add `KEEPTTL` or a fresh expiry option.
